children.text: The following facts about surface tension may turn out to be useful for this problem. For the molecules of a liquid, positions at the liquid-air interface are less favourable than positions in the bulk. This interface is described by the surface energy \(U=\sigma S\), where \(S\) is the surface area of the interface and \(\sigma\) is the surface-tension coefficient. Moreover, two fragments of the liquid surface pull each other with a force \(F=\sigma l\), where \(l\) is the length of a straight line separating the fragments.

children.text: A long metallic pipe with internal diameter \(d\) is pointing directly downwards. Water is slowly dripping from a nozzle at its lower end. Water can be considered electrically conducting, with surface tension \(\sigma\) and density \(\rho\). A droplet of radius \(r\) hangs below the nozzle. The radius grows slowly until the droplet separates from the nozzle due to the free-fall acceleration \(g\). Always assume \(d\ll r\).
Find the radius \(r_{\max}\) of a drop just before it separates from the nozzle.
Relative to the far-away surroundings, the pipe's electrostatic potential is \(\varphi\). Find the charge \(Q\) of a drop when its radius is \(r\).

Consider the situation in which \(r\) is kept constant and \(\varphi\) is slowly increased. The droplet becomes unstable and breaks into pieces if the hydrostatic pressure inside the droplet becomes smaller than atmospheric pressure. Find the critical potential \(\varphi_{\max}\) at which this happens.

An apparatus called the Kelvin water dropper consists of two pipes, each identical to the one described in Part A, connected via a T-junction. The ends of both pipes are at the centres of two cylindrical electrodes with height \(L\) and diameter \(D\), where \(L\gg D\gg r\). For both tubes, the dripping rate is \(n\) droplets per unit time. Droplets fall from height \(H\) into conductive bowls underneath the nozzles, cross-connected to the electrodes as shown. The electrodes are connected via a capacitance \(C\). There is no net charge on the system of bowls and electrodes. The top water container is earthed. The first droplet to fall has some microscopic charge which causes an imbalance between the two sides and a small charge separation across the capacitor.

nodes.alt: Original Kelvin dropper wiring: earthed top reservoir feeding two nozzles, cylindrical electrodes of height L and diameter D connected by capacitance C, and crossed connections from each electrode to the opposite collecting bowl a distance H below.

children.text: Express the absolute value of the charge \(Q_0\) of the drops as they separate from the tubes, at the instant when the capacitor's charge is \(q\). Express \(Q_0\) in terms of \(r_{\max}\) from Part A.i and neglect the effect described in Part A.iii.
Find the dependence of \(q\) on time \(t\) by approximating it with a continuous function \(q(t)\), assuming \(q(0)=q_0\).

The dropper's functioning can be hindered by the effect shown in Part A.iii. In addition, a limit \(U_{\max}\) to the achievable potential between the electrodes is set by the electrostatic push between a droplet and the bowl beneath it. Find \(U_{\max}\).

statement.text:
Kelvin water dropper (8 points)
The following facts about surface tension may turn out to be useful for this problem. For the molecules of a liquid, positions at the liquid-air interface are less favourable than positions in the bulk. This interface is described by the surface energy \(U=\sigma S\), where \(S\) is the surface area of the interface and \(\sigma\) is the surface-tension coefficient. Moreover, two fragments of the liquid surface pull each other with a force \(F=\sigma l\), where \(l\) is the length of a straight line separating the fragments.

A long metallic pipe with internal diameter \(d\) is pointing directly downwards. Water is slowly dripping from a nozzle at its lower end. Water can be considered electrically conducting, with surface tension \(\sigma\) and density \(\rho\). A droplet of radius \(r\) hangs below the nozzle. The radius grows slowly until the droplet separates from the nozzle due to the free-fall acceleration \(g\). Always assume \(d\ll r\).
Part A. Single pipe (4 points)
A.i (1.2 points)
Find the radius \(r_{\max}\) of a drop just before it separates from the nozzle.
A.ii (1.2 points)
Relative to the far-away surroundings, the pipe's electrostatic potential is \(\varphi\). Find the charge \(Q\) of a drop when its radius is \(r\).
A.iii (1.6 points)
Consider the situation in which \(r\) is kept constant and \(\varphi\) is slowly increased. The droplet becomes unstable and breaks into pieces if the hydrostatic pressure inside the droplet becomes smaller than atmospheric pressure. Find the critical potential \(\varphi_{\max}\) at which this happens.
Part B. Two pipes (4 points)
An apparatus called the Kelvin water dropper consists of two pipes, each identical to the one described in Part A, connected via a T-junction. The ends of both pipes are at the centres of two cylindrical electrodes with height \(L\) and diameter \(D\), where \(L\gg D\gg r\). For both tubes, the dripping rate is \(n\) droplets per unit time. Droplets fall from height \(H\) into conductive bowls underneath the nozzles, cross-connected to the electrodes as shown. The electrodes are connected via a capacitance \(C\). There is no net charge on the system of bowls and electrodes. The top water container is earthed. The first droplet to fall has some microscopic charge which causes an imbalance between the two sides and a small charge separation across the capacitor.

B.i (1.2 points)
Express the absolute value of the charge \(Q_0\) of the drops as they separate from the tubes, at the instant when the capacitor's charge is \(q\). Express \(Q_0\) in terms of \(r_{\max}\) from Part A.i and neglect the effect described in Part A.iii.
B.ii (1.5 points)
Find the dependence of \(q\) on time \(t\) by approximating it with a continuous function \(q(t)\), assuming \(q(0)=q_0\).
B.iii (1.3 points)
The dropper's functioning can be hindered by the effect shown in Part A.iii. In addition, a limit \(U_{\max}\) to the achievable potential between the electrodes is set by the electrostatic push between a droplet and the bowl beneath it. Find \(U_{\max}\).

solution.text:
Part A. Single pipe
A.i
Write the force balance for the droplet. Since \(d\ll r\), the force \(\pi\Delta p\,d^2/4\) from the excess pressure inside the tube is negligible. Gravity, \(4\pi r_{\max}^3\rho g/3\), is balanced by the capillary force. Just before separation, the water forms a neck with a vertical tangent near the nozzle. The capillary force across the neck's horizontal cross-section is \(\pi\sigma d\), so
\[r_{\max}=\sqrt[3]{\frac{3\sigma d}{4\rho g}}.\]
A.ii
Since \(d\ll r\), the tube's effect on the droplet capacitance is negligible. Its potential is both \(\varphi\) and \(Q/(4\pi\epsilon_0r)\), hence
\[Q=4\pi\epsilon_0\varphi r.\]
A.iii
The excess pressure is the sum of capillary pressure \(2\sigma/r\), which increases the pressure, and electrostatic pressure \(\epsilon_0 E^2/2=\epsilon_0\varphi^2/(2r^2)\), which decreases it. The excess pressure changes sign when
\[\frac{\epsilon_0\varphi_{\max}^2}{2r^2}=\frac{2\sigma}{r},\qquad\varphi_{\max}=2\sqrt{\frac{\sigma r}{\epsilon_0}}.\]
The source derives the electrostatic pressure as follows. A surface charge of density \(\sigma\) and area \(S\) feels \(F=\sigma S\bar E\), where \(\bar E\) excludes that surface element's own field. The force is perpendicular to the surface, so \(F/S\) is a pressure. Gauss's law gives the field jump \(\Delta E=\sigma/\epsilon_0\). The field inside the conductor vanishes: \(\bar E-\Delta E/2=0\). Outside, \(E=\bar E+\Delta E/2\). Thus \(\bar E=E/2=\Delta E/2\), giving the stated pressure. Here the source reuses the symbol sigma for surface charge density.
Alternatively, consider a virtual displacement of a capacitor's surface and compare pressure work \(p\Delta V\) with the change in electric-field energy \(\epsilon_0E^2\Delta V/2\).
A third derivation requires the mechanical work \(dA\), also denoted \(dW\) in the source, for an infinitesimal droplet inflation to vanish. Energy conservation gives
\[dW+dW_{\mathrm{el}}=\sigma\,d(4\pi r^2)+\frac12\varphi_{\max}^2\,dC_d,\qquad C_d=4\pi\epsilon_0r,\]
\[dW_{\mathrm{el}}=\varphi_{\max}\,dq=4\pi\epsilon_0\varphi_{\max}^2\,dr.\]
Setting \(dW=0\) recovers the same critical potential.
Part B. Two pipes
B.i
Relative to the surrounding electrode, whose potential is \(-U/2\) with \(U=q/C\), the earthed droplet is at \(U/2\). Either sign convention is acceptable if used consistently. The long cylindrical electrode effectively shields the potential of the external surroundings. Using Part A
\[Q=2\pi\epsilon_0Ur_{\max}=\frac{2\pi\epsilon_0qr_{\max}}C.\]
B.ii
The droplet's charge has the same sign as the capacitor's opposite plate, connected to the farther electrode. Falling into the bowl therefore increases the capacitor charge by \(Q\)
\[dq=2\pi\epsilon_0Ur_{\max}\,dN=\frac{2\pi\epsilon_0r_{\max}n}{C}q\,dt,\qquad dN=n\,dt.\]
Solving this linear differential equation
\[q=q_0e^{\gamma t},\qquad\gamma=\frac{2\pi\epsilon_0r_{\max}n}{C}=\frac{\pi\epsilon_0n}{C}\sqrt[3]{\frac{6\sigma d}{\rho g}}.\]
B.iii
The droplets reach the bowls if their mechanical energy \(mgH\), with \(m\) the droplet mass, overcomes the electric repulsion. The initial total potential is zero: the electrode contributes \(U/2\), while the droplet itself contributes \(-U/2\). Its motion is not affected by its own field, so the external potential changes from \(U/2\) to \(-U/2\). The change in electrostatic energy obeys \(UQ\le mgH\), with \(Q=2\pi\epsilon_0Ur_{\max}\). Therefore
\[U_{\max}=\frac{mgH}{2\pi\epsilon_0U_{\max}r_{\max}},\]
\[U_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{H\sigma d}{2\epsilon_0r_{\max}}}=\sqrt[6]{\frac{H^3g\sigma^2\rho d^2}{6\epsilon_0^3}}.\]
